An equipment upgrade appears to have brought airline departures across the U.S. to a standstill Friday , raising questions about how the nation’s air traffic control network is being modernized — and whether safeguards should have prevented the disruption.
The nationwide ground stop — the longest since the September 11 attacks — led to 14,000 flights cancellations Friday and Saturday as the disruption and its aftermath spread through airline schedules. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed an “incredibly old air traffic control system,” saying communications equipment became “overloaded with data” and “went down.” By Saturday, he pointed more specifically to routine work replacing copper telecommunications wiring with fiber .
Aviation experts said precautions should have prevented an equipment change from overwhelming the network, leading to scrutiny over installation procedures and preparations for recovering when an upgrade goes wrong.
The disruption has also intensified a funding debate , with Duffy seeking another $50 billion after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. But experts caution that new equipment alone cannot eliminate failures in a sprawling system that must remain operational throughout its overhaul.
“A large-scale modernization, no matter how warranted and well-intended, cannot solve all these problems. This is a system that runs 24/7, 365 days a year. We cannot turn it off while we build a new one and then start a new one from scratch,” David Lovell, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at the University of Maryland, told The Independent .
“Any modernization will, by necessity, be done piecemeal. That will mean integrating new subsystems with old subsystems, with the consequent interfaces at the boundaries that are often points of vulnerability,” he added.
Air traffic controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and aircraft communications at 3:36 p.m. Friday, Duffy said. Eighteen minutes later, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop , barring departures as officials sought to identify the problem.
The order was lifted at 8:15 p.m., but airlines continued struggling to restore their schedules. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, with thousands more canceled or delayed Saturday, leaving thousands of passengers stranded at airports across the U.S.
Duffy said Saturday that contractor L3Harris may have installed a faulty router — a device that directs information through a network — at a site in Arkansas . The work involved replacing copper wires, which carry electrical signals, with fiber optic cables, which can transmit more data over longer distances.
L3Harris has partnered with the federal government for a decade and is replacing the Federal Aviation Administration’s copper wires with fiber-optic cables. FAA and company officials are working in L3Harris’ Florida lab to analyze the router at the center of the stop.
“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” the company said in a statement.
The company’s work comes the nation has long sought to upgrade its decade-old air traffic control system. Edward Booth, an aviation attorney and pilot based in Jacksonville, Florida, told Time Magazine that billions of dollars have already been sunk into the process.
“It's a very highly technical, robust system,” Booth says of the National Airspace System (NAS), “but it seems the weak spot was discovered yesterday afternoon.”
An overload can affect facilities around the country that exchange radar information and voice communications, said Hassan Shahidi, president and CEO of the Flight Safety Foundation.
“It appears to have been a system overload caused by this new router,” he told The Independent .
Lance Sherry, a professor of systems engineering at George Mason University, said air traffic control comprises three interacting networks: communications, navigation and surveillance. Their connections help explain how a local problem can spread to a nationwide shutdown.
“For this reason we consider [air traffic control] to be a network-of-networks,” Sherry said. “A perturbation in one location of the network can, under the right circumstances, propagate through the network.”
Independent industry analyst Bob Mann noted that the FAA had recently expanded its SMART traffic-management platform nationwide. The AI-assisted tool, which helps FAA staff plan traffic flows, was rolled out nationally three days before the ground stop.
Federal officials, however, have said this new tool was not responsible for the outage.
Lovell said the disruption should not obscure the safety response.
“The safety aspects of the system performed admirably,” he told The Independent . “The procedures to get aircraft out of the air safely worked perfectly, and there was no loss of life or bodily injury.”
The FAA and its telecommunications provider should have safeguards to prevent an equipment change from overwhelming the network, Shahidi said. Preliminary findings pointed to a router setting that apparently allowed it to send excessive information.
“This particular router has a feature that has a broader broadcast capability. That feature apparently was not disabled,” he said.
While investigators were still establishing the cause, he argued that appropriate settings, testing and training should block such an overload. “This is something that I believe is preventable,” he said.
The FAA has already replaced more than 3,500 copper communications lines with fiber-optic connections, out of 5,170 scheduled for replacement by 2028.
With many more upgrades ahead, Shahidi said understanding what went wrong and preparing for future installations is essential. “They need to have a plan, a backup plan,” he said.
The disruption has sharpened a dispute over whether the FAA needs more money or a better plan for spending what it already has. The administration says existing funding cannot cover a full overhaul, while Democrats are demanding an accounting of unspent money and a clearer explanation of what another $50 billion would buy.
Congress approved $12.5 billion for modernization last year, which Duffy has described as a down payment rather than the full cost of replacing outdated systems. By Friday, he increased that request to $50 billion, calling the need an “emergency.”
“This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said Friday.
President Donald Trump took a more partisan approach in Sunday Truth Social posts, accusing the Biden administration of making an “ old and broken system worse than when they began .” He urged Congress to approve funding rather than modernizing in “drips and drabs.”
Democrats say their objections are not to modernization itself, but to the administration’s management of the effort. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said previously approved funding largely remained unspent and accused Duffy of demanding “a $50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver.”
“Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner,” she said in a statement.
Beyond the funding dispute lies a separate question: whether replacing old equipment would prevent another disruption similar to Friday’s. Lovell said the suspected involvement of newly installed routers complicated that argument.

articles.title_zh: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.content_orig:

SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
For years, Ukraine has had a bull’s-eye on the only bridge linking the occupied Crimean Peninsula to Russia.
After Moscow used Crimea as a springboard to launch its all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Kyiv bombed the bridge that year with explosives hidden in a truck. The next year, Ukraine attacked it with unmanned naval vessels . Two years after that, it dispatched covert operatives to try to bring the bridge down by planting explosives on undersea support pillars.
The 12-mile-long structure, the Kerch Strait Bridge, survived it all, a powerful if scarred symbol of Moscow’s control of Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014 . But before dawn on Tuesday, Ukraine struck its biggest blow yet, sending a significant section of the bridge into the sea after a series of drone and missile attacks.
In a statement about the bridge, the Ukrainian military command said, “Russia built a myth around it as a symbol of Crimea being ‘Russian forever.’”
“Now,” the statement added, “part of the structure lies in the water.”
The Ukrainian government released photographs and video documenting the attack and aftermath. The New York Times also verified social media video showing the collapse of a central span of the bridge used for vehicle traffic.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia earnings live updates: Wall Street braces for first report since Huang's ouster
articles.title_zh: Nvidia earnings live updates: Wall Street braces for first report since Huang's ouster
articles.content_orig:
In his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO last week, Jensen Huang struck a contrite tone, saying that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence contact.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in the written statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
Huang said he had seen support from investors and employees and was willing to come back as CEO to help the company navigate "complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I  would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in the statement.
Sources told CNBC Monday that the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO.
Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO, putting together an online petition with over 180,000 signatures.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Jensen Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia.
Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang, Nvidia's founder, admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia.
Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. Its board of directors said on Friday that it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.
Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
Here is the entire statement from Huang:
Over the past week, I've been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry  colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the  greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life's work. Building it  into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor.  Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I  love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious  mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my  mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent  investigation.
Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my  return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I  would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
CORRECTION: Jensen Huang is the former CEO of Nvidia. His title was misstated in a headline on an earlier version of this article.

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives just as Southeast Asian summit is ending, but still looms over talks
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives just as Southeast Asian summit is ending, but still looms over talks
articles.content_orig:
President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
After landing in Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific region, a relationship Mr. Trump described as "very special." Those nations are Australia, India and Japan, as well as the United States.
Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."
There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip , with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.
Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."
Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China. After arriving, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."
The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders , is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.
Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.
In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.
On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.
As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.
Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang , the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.
Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.
"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.
When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.
The Nvidia Board of Directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."
Seiji  Yamashita contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (Â£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
Putin (centre) personally opened the Crimean Bridge by driving a lorry over it in May 2018
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
Images show the damage to the Crimean Bridge from the overnight attack
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Watch: BBC reports from Kyiv bridge hit by Russian attack
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

President Donald Trumparrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila , the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin , and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un .
Trump administration details its $50 billion request for aviation system improvements
The Trump administration has formally updated its request to lawmakers for $50.1 billion to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system and to make other improvements at airports.
A letter to key lawmakers dated Tuesday says that less than 24 hours after the administration’s request of $30.1 billion, “the urgent need for this investment became undeniable.” That’s when outdated equipment disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds, forcing the Federal Aviation Administration to initiate a nationwide ground stop.
The request to lawmakers calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation’s air traffic control system. Another $10 billion would go to boosting airport infrastructure.
Meanwhile, $10 billion would go to replace or refurbish terminals at high-impact hubs. Another $10 billion would go to construct five new traffic control centers and $10 billion would go to improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
Trump’s pick to lead the Navy focuses on shipbuilding in his opening statements
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told senators at his confirmation hearing Tuesday that he’ll focus on revitalizing shipbuilding in an effort to expand the nation’s fleet of warships.
But Cao avoided potentially thorny topics that are likely to come up before the Senate Armed Services Committee. Those include the Iran war, the recent firings of Navy admirals and the waiver Cao will need from Congress to become Navy secretary because he left active duty less than seven years ago.
Cao also spoke of his biography, which includes fleeing Vietnam with his family right before the fall of Saigon in the 1970s. He also focused on his 25 years of service in the Navy.
“I spent my entire adult life serving in the United States Navy special operations community with multiple combat deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia,” Cao said.
Bipartisan concerns arise over forces being ‘stretched thin’ during Navy secretary hearing
Despite deep divisions over the Iran war, the Republican and Democratic leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee voiced a unified concern over the impact the ongoing military operation and internal issues at the Department of Defense have had on the U.S. Navy.
“Our sailors and Marines are our greatest asset, but they cannot sustain an increasingly demanding operational tempo without adequate support,” GOP Sen. Roger Wicker, the committee chair, said during his opening statement.
His Democratic counterpart, Sen. Jack Reed, echoed his worry, saying that “disruption” from high-ranking officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, “sends the wrong signal to our sailors and Marines.”
Confirmation hearing for Trump’s nominee to lead the US Navy gets underway
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, appeared Tuesday before the Senate Armed Services Committee as he seeks the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. It’s the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Cao also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
ASEAN-US dinner menu features American surf and turf
The main course was a pairing of U.S. beef tenderloin and lobster tail, served with a truffle potato puree, glazed baby carrots, oyster mushrooms and a wine sauce, according to details shared by the White House.
Courses before the main included ratatouille, goose liver mousse and burrata cheese salad with heirloom tomatoes, walnuts, balsamic glaze and olive oil.
Chocolate-covered cake with roasted almonds and salted caramel ice cream was served for dessert.
Trump’s pick for Navy secretary likely to face Iran war questions during confirmation hearing
He’s scheduled to testify before a Senate committee Tuesday, the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, is seeking the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. He also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
Cao will face the current Congress, with Republicans still in charge. But he’s likely to face intense scrutiny from Democrats over aspects of the Iran war, including major damage to the service’s 5th Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, as well as the recent firings of Navy officials.
Trump could meet Imelda Marcos during summit in Philippines
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion between Trump and an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she’s well enough and gets her doctors’ nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet-set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 “People Power” public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: “How’s Imelda?” Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
“Personal connections are very important to him,” Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. “President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, ‘Please say hello to your mother,’” according to Romualdez.
US and Thailand sign joint statement affirming terms of forthcoming trade deal
At a brief signing ceremony in Manila, Trump said Thailand has agreed to eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove “substantial” nontariff barriers on American automobiles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry.
Trump said Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products and “that makes our farmers very happy.”
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said there’s still “a little more to do” before the agreement itself is finalized and that it should be “ready for us to sign real soon.”
Trump still talking about possible meetings with Russia, North Korea leaders
Trump says North Korea’s leader would like to meet with him in China later this week. And he’s open to sitting down with Russian President Vladimir Putin, too.
But so far, it appears neither meeting has been arranged.
Trump landed in the Philippines on Tuesday for talks with Asia-Pacific leaders. On Thursday, he’s due in Shenzhen, China, for more talks, including a historic three-way confab with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia’s CEO
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang said Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return to his job as CEO of Nvidia if the chip giant’s board of directors decided to bring him back.
In a statement posted to X , Huang, who resigned as CEO last week over allegations of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, said he would welcome the opportunity to retake the reins of the company he co-founded in 1993.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang also said he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.”
“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret,” he said. “I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”
A portion of the statement was first reported by The Wall Street Journal, prompting shares of Nvidia to erase their earlier losses.
Earlier Tuesday, Republicans announced that Huang had agreed to sit for an interview with several House committees about whether the computer chip giant’s sales to China may have endangered U.S. national security.
Huang is set to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee on Dec. 1.  Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter will sit for an interview the following day.
Their remarks will not be publicly televised but will be transcribed and could be released at a later date.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” the chairmen of the three committees — Republican Reps. Brian Mast of Florida, John Moolenaar of Michigan and Rick Crawford of Arkansas — said in a joint statement Tuesday.
“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” they wrote referring to the People’s Republic of China.
Nvidia has previously denied violating any national security laws and said that it makes every effort to comply with protocols for overseas sales.
“We look forward to meeting with the Chairmen on December 2,” an Nvidia spokesperson said in an email, notably referring only to the date of Teter’s interview, and not Huang’s.
Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week following allegations of extramarital relationships, including one with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. The company is expected to report quarterly earnings following the market close Tuesday.

articles.title_zh: Trump meets key US regional allies in Manila ahead of China visit
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .

GUANGZHOU, China — Behind the scenes, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spent months pushing for action that would signal resolve within the Trump administration against China’s pursuit of the most powerful American computer chips, a flashpoint in their race for superiority in artificial intelligence, multiple sources said.
But Trump’s courtship of Xi Jinping, seeking to alleviate tensions among the world’s greatest powers, and a contingent of advisors skeptical of commercial warfare against Beijing slowed the process down — giving China months of opportunity to gain access to U.S. semiconductors through the back door.
Ultimately, just hours before departing for Asia alongside President Trump, Bessent got his way, bolstering his position ahead of talks with Chinese officials in Shenzhen this week on the risks posed by frontier systems.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit, that Washington is serious about curbing Chinese circumvention — and that China hawks within the administration may be gaining the upper hand.
Trump has repeatedly sidestepped confrontation with Xi over the intensifying AI race in their two previous meetings this year, in Beijing and Washington, wary of upsetting a carefully managed détente and reluctant to jeopardize a technology boom increasingly central to the U.S. economy.
The new rules restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best AI models.
But the administration, from the president down, is acutely aware of China’s ambitions to dominate an industry that could reshape the global balance of power. That competitive drive was underscored this month by a scandal involving a Chinese espionage campaign targeting Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia, the world’s leading AI chip maker.
Before resigning from the company in disgrace over the weekend, Huang admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy — a woman who worked at a Singaporean firm accused by American authorities of helping to divert restricted Nvidia chips to China, in violation of U.S. export controls.
The national security scandal has roiled the markets — and in so doing, commanded Trump’s attention — inflicting a significant devaluation on Nvidia and reverberating well beyond it, wiping nearly $1 trillion from the combined market value of major technology companies in a single trading session on Monday.
Trump, who counts Huang a friend and ally, indicated he would be open to his return as Nvidia’s chief executive . Bessent suggested otherwise, expressing confidence its board could find competent new leadership and urging a full investigation.
Trump is not expected to raise the Nvidia matter directly with Xi. But Bessent plans to do so in his own meetings, one official said.
The Treasury secretary has thus taken on the role of an enforcer, pursuing a tougher line than Trump is willing to take himself in his highly personalized relationship with the Chinese leader.
Bessent is scheduled to meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on the sidelines of the summitry in Shenzhen to discuss potential collaboration on AI safety protocols, standards for testing of advanced models, and a direct communications channel for AI emergencies.
The two men have met before to discuss AI, most recently in New York, where they agreed in principle to coordinate. But the talks have yet to produce much in the way of tangible results.
“Bessent is signaling that, while he sees working with Beijing to mitigate AI risks as a priority, it won’t come at the expense of actions that he sees as necessary to protect U.S. national security, like limiting AI chip exports to China,” said Daniel Remler, a senior fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
The administration’s latest action marks a policy defeat for Howard Lutnick , secretary of the Commerce Department, who oversees chip policy and had advocated for a less restrictive approach than Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative.
The feud began spilling into public view ahead of the president’s travel, and in light of the Nvidia scandal, after Bessent said in a television interview that the Commerce Department “has the pen” to act, implying a split within the team.
“Look, there’re two different views,” Trump told reporters on Monday, answering questions on the matter. “One view is you don’t want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
“The other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do,” Trump continued. “You can’t say either is wrong or right. We’ll let you know.”
Beyond the diplomatic niceties, Trump has been explicit and consistent since resuming office that the United States must “win” the race for AI superiority, calling the alternative “not acceptable.”
“Whoever wins AI,” Trump said at the UN General Assembly in September, “whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”
Trump will arrive in China on Wednesday after meeting with world leaders in Manila, including those from the Quad — an alliance of Japan, India, Australia and the United States — which discussed AI at their own summit Tuesday evening.
Describing “superintelligence” — Trump’s preferred term for AI — as “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution,” Trump announced a Quad effort to accelerate adoption of the technology, including an investment of more than $85 million to enhance AI ecosystems throughout the region.
“We want to be careful with it,” Trump said, “but it’s amazing, the things that have come out, in terms of science and in terms of medical breakthroughs. No one can believe what we’re finding. And we’re finding it fast.”
“We want to be very careful, but we want to cherish it,” he added. “The United States as you know is leading in that capacity, by quite a bit.”
As he meets with the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, Trump will face pressure to sustain resolve against Beijing despite his yearlong courtship of President Xi Jinping.
The new U.S. rule requires overseas data centers serving customers in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba to identify their end users before gaining access to chips. It also imposes additional licensing requirements on chip sales to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the Commerce Department identifies as posing a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations.
U.S. officials say that export controls are not up for negotiation in talks with the Chinese. But Beijing sees them as yet another historic example of Washington trying to contain its rise — a posture that has repeatedly stifled diplomatic progress between the two superpowers.
“While administration officials say export controls aren’t up for negotiation, Chinese officials will certainly bring them up,” Remler said. “These restrictions are the key obstacle to China’s AI progress, which is increasingly important to the Chinese economy and to Xi’s strategic goals.”

articles.title_orig: Tech outages live updates: Microsoft, banks and FAA
articles.title_zh: Tech outages live updates: Microsoft, banks and FAA
articles.content_orig:
PHOENIX (AZFamily) — A software bug blocked customers from their accounts at several major banks Monday in Arizona and across the country, the third technology failure in days.
Tim Roemer, the former director of the Arizona Department of Homeland Security, does not think the failures are a coincidence.
“It really seems like these are self-inflicted wounds,” he said.
Last Thursday, a global outage of Microsoft outlook impacted millions of users and disrupted business communications, police crime reporting, and court operations.
Then the next day, airports across Arizona, and the country, were impacted by a communications issue that forced an hours-long nationwide ground stop .
“There’s a couple hundred thousand tech employees that have lost their jobs around the world these last couple years and now, we’re having all these technology failures, all of these bugs, all of these patching issues,” Roemer said. “The software problems are a direct tie to this. There’s just no doubt about it.”
Roemer said growing technology responsibly will be the key as the country becomes more reliant on it.
“There’s a lot of 16-year-olds right now driving around in Ferraris, and that is a comparison to what’s happening in AI and the tech sector,” Roemer said.
Investigations are underway to determine exactly what went wrong in the three separate failures in days.
Roemer warned that more outages are likely no matter what investigators find, but that we shouldn’t panic when they happen.
“We as a society almost need to get used to this to a certain extent, which is sad, but it’s like, if we’re going to rely on technology for everything in our lives we have to be prepared for the speed bumps,” Roemer says. “And I think as society, if we’re responsible and we take just basic precautions, we’ll be resilient.”
Roemer said the way to be resilient is to be prepared. Which could mean bringing extra medication if you need to the airport, having cash in case banks get impacted again, or having multiple ways to get in contact with certain people in case email is affected.

articles.title_orig: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.title_zh: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services, though Chase said its issue has now been resolved.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems was behind the glitch and it was not a cyber security incident.
A spokesperson said "this was not a systemic issue" but noted the impact may have affected other banks "only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us".
The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights .
In addition, United Airlines also reported a "widespread system outage".
The problems with the banks started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.
Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News, though Chase Bank told the BBC that customers still had access to their accounts and funds.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.
Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".
The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.
The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.
Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.
Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.
US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.
Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.
Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.
As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.
Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".
That issue resolved within a few hours.
The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.
The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.
The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , but comes as other industries report different outages around the US.
On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues.
The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.

Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome
WASHINGTON -- Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.
The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook's lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov. 6 . Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed's board of governors, a charge she denies.
President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president's efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed's independence and reflect Trump's desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.
“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.”
In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.”
Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a Nov. 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating.
The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Labor Secretary.
The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions.
Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause,” but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was asked at a press conference Oct. 28 if he or the Fed would be involved in the hearing against Cook, and he said, “not to my knowledge.”

articles.title_orig: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.title_zh: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.content_orig:
Sentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices.
Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38.
Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%.
Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020.
"Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."
More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them  reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them.
"The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges,  including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back."
In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23.

articles.title_orig: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
articles.title_zh: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
articles.content_orig:
Gulf states have been worried for weeks that Iran may again begin to target them in an effort to force a resolution to the nine-month regional conflict on its terms.
In the past few days, that anxiety has deepened with two attempted drone attacks on Bahrain, an American ally that hosts major US military facilities, while Tehran has also warned the Gulf states not to “reopen old wounds.”
Iran appears to be raising the stakes as it struggles to prevent more Gulf oil and gas from getting through the Strait of Hormuz as its economy labors under US blockade and the cumulative effect of international sanctions.
The Bahrain Defense Force said Sunday it had “intercepted and destroyed” several Iranian drones, after a similar interception on Friday.
The US Embassy in Bahrain on Sunday urged Americans to exercise “heightened vigilance,” citing an increased threat of attacks by Iran-backed Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US government officials and facilities in the region. The embassy also warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions, while noting that it remained open.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had earlier claimed an attack on a US helicopter base in Bahrain, saying it was in retaliation for unspecified US “aggression.” CNN has reached out to US Central Command for comment.
The targeting of Bahrain has been accompanied by a more belligerent tone out of Tehran toward Iran’s neighbors, the consequences of renewed US or Israeli strikes and the state of negotiations with the US.
Iran was incensed by suggestions from the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) last week that it would have to pay its neighbors compensation for attacks on their territory, something Iran itself is seeking in any deal with the US.
“How can countries that actively participated in military aggression against a neighboring country and made their airspace, territory and waters available to those who attacked Iranian territory speak of seeking compensation from Iran?” asked Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei in a news conference on Sunday.
“What about Iran’s inherent and legal right to defend itself?”
In a reminder that Iran does not forget the past, Baghaei said the Gulf states “must be careful not to reopen old wounds,” referring to their support for Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in the war with Iran in the 1980s.
Iran wants the Gulf states “to pay the price for a war they did not choose, then give up their right to accountability and compensation. This is an equation that cannot be accepted,” said Ebtesam Al-Ketbi, of the Emirates Policy Center think tank, on Sunday.
A sign of growing unease about the prospect of renewed hostilities came last week when the GCC announced an advanced headquarters in Kuwait for its unified military command and the deployment of forces to the facility.
The organization’s secretary general, Jasem Mohamed Al Budaiwi, said the move showed “a firm Gulf commitment to safeguarding the security and sovereignty of the GCC states” following what he called “heinous Iranian attacks.”
Iran has also stepped up attacks on shipping in the Gulf, with almost daily claims – few of them substantiated – that tankers have struck mines as they’ve tried to transit the Strait of Hormuz.
For Tehran, the increase in Gulf energy exports to close to pre-war levels in recent weeks, and the sharp decline in oil prices, deprive it of vital leverage in negotiations. The International Energy Agency said Gulf oil exports - excluding Oman - reached 18.4 million barrels a day in October, about 26% below prewar levels.
At the same time, Iran has been unable to export any meaningful amount of its own crude for more than two months.
The Iranian regime is demanding an end to the US blockade, the progressive removal of international sanctions and an unfreezing of billions of dollars in frozen assets as conditions for resuming negotiations with the US.
But US President Donald Trump appears content to let the economic squeeze on Iran take its course, anticipating that Tehran will have to soften its terms and recognizing the Gulf states want to avoid another round of conflict.
“At the request of the nations that I am ⁠looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly,” Trump said Thursday. At the same time, he canceled efforts by Vice President JD Vance to resurrect talks with Iran, declaring: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.”
Indeed, Iran’s economic pain appears to be deepening even as senior officials in Tehran insist it can withstand the pressure and can access hard currency to support the rial, whose value has fallen drastically since the conflict began.
One perpetual sign of hardship is the long lines seen at gas stations in many parts of Iran.
Esmail Saghab Esfahani, a vice president, acknowledged last week that there was a supply problem and that Iranians could no longer count on fuel stations to meet their needs.
Some residents of the port city of Bandar Abbas blocked traffic on Thursday to protest against fuel shortages. The speaker of the Iranian parliament, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, suggested officials stop talking about the fuel issue, always sensitive in Iran.
And yet there are no public indications the regime is ready to compromise.
Baghaei was asked Sunday whether Iran would accept a temporary suspension of uranium enrichment or a reduction in enrichment levels in negotiations with Washington.
“No. We are not at that stage at all. During this period, we are not discussing any details related to the nuclear issue, nor have we held any such discussions.”
Ghalibaf said Sunday it made no difference whether Washington wanted negotiations or war.
“If the Americans make another mistake this time, the capabilities and will of Iran’s armed forces will determine the geography of the battlefield.”
Iran has frequently warned that another chapter in the conflict will see it broaden targets to infrastructure across the region, including subsea cables.
Additionally, its Houthi allies in Yemen fire ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia almost daily and appear to have put Saudi-backed government forces under renewed pressure in the south of Yemen, forcing them to retreat from near the Red Sea in a setback in their campaign.
The result is an unstable limbo across the region.
“The United States may believe it can maintain the blockade for an extended period, but Iran sees it as a direct threat to its economy, sovereignty, and national security,” Israeli analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies, wrote on X.
The US “cannot assume that time alone will force Tehran to surrender. Iran has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to absorb enormous economic costs rather than abandon what its leadership considers fundamental national interests.”

articles.content_orig:
The president is headed this week to summits in the Philippines and China that will include a meeting with Xi Jinping and a trilateral meeting with Xi and Vladimir Putin.
President Donald Trump heads to China later this week for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on trade and denuclearization, but one topic that won’t be on Trump’s agenda, according to U.S. officials, is Nvidia.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation after an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sent political shock waves through Washington. Trump confirmed that the FBI was looking into the case, and lawmakers are demanding answers about whether China was able to access Nvidia’s advanced computer chips, which are used for artificial intelligence.
Leaving the White House Monday morning, the president said “I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy” as he downplayed national security concerns. “It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China. But our country now militarily is stronger than we’ve ever been,” Trump told reporters. The president also said he “wouldn’t mind” if Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO, but added he may talk to Xi about the spying allegations.
Still, despite the growing number of questions about Nvidia, a U.S. official who previewed the president’s trip to reporters in a background call Friday said it “should not really have any bearing on the trip in all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese.”
“I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it’s probably not something that we’re going to read the Chinese in on at this moment,” the U.S. official said.
Those questions about China’s access to advanced computer chips spilled out into the public last week. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not implementing stricter controls on exports of Nvidia chips to Megaspeed International, a company run by the alleged Chinese spy. Beijing has denied the espionage allegations.
The White House has expressed “complete confidence” in Lutnick, and a Department of Commerce spokesperson told MS NOW, “Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions.”
“These are national security matters that we develop in the administration,” the U.S. official said on the call, adding that it was an “interagency process” and that officials “don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there.” The official did say the U.S. was discussing closing “loopholes” in existing measures to control exports of advanced AI chips to China.
The president’s trip to Asia includes two international summits: first in Manila, Philippines, to meet with leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, followed by Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen, China. Accompanying the president, according to the White House are Bessent, Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett and U.S. Trade representative Jamieson Greer.
Last week Trump called Huang’s resignation a “horrible thing” and said he didn’t plan to raise the situation with the Chinese leader. But the president added, “I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. I mean, he built a great company.”
In May, Huang accompanied Trump on a trip to China for a state visit. It was on that trip that Rubio briefed Trump about Huang’s alleged connection to a suspected Chinese spy, according to a U.S. official granted anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence information. Trump has denied that he received that warning, which was first reported by The New York Times.
A second U.S. official on Friday’s preview call told reporters that SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk was expected to accompany Trump to Asia. The U.S. official said that Musk would be traveling as an adviser given his “tremendous business interests” in the U.S.-China relationship and that he was a “big part of our national security.”
One area Trump is expected to confront Xi over is China’s growing nuclear arsenal.
Previewing a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, a second U.S. official briefing reporters on the same call said it was time for China to “step up” to the “adult table” on nuclear nonproliferation talks. While Russia and the U.S. have larger stockpiles, the official criticized China’s rapid nuclear development, adding that “things that China is doing very opaquely with their nuclear arsenals” affect the “security of every human being in the world.”
The official added that the administration was not expecting any immediate denuclearization agreement from the trilateral meeting, stressing that the occasion would serve as the “entry point” for further efforts to reduce the number of nuclear weapons.
The three leaders are also expected to discuss the war with Iran, according to the U.S. official. Both China and Russia have provided an economic lifeline to Iran through their existing trade relationships, but Trump has downplayed any significant military support to Tehran.
There are no plans for a bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin at the APEC summit. The U.S. official said the president did not plan to discuss the war in Ukraine in the trilateral meeting given separate ongoing negotiations being led by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Musk, whose Starlink system has been used in the war by Ukraine, will not attend the trilateral meeting, the U.S. official said.
Trump told reporters Monday he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The president didn’t offer any additional information other than a potential meeting would take place in China.
After visiting Beijing in May, this will be Trump’s second trip to China this year, and his third meeting with Xi in as much time. Two months ago the Chinese president visited Trump at the White House. The trilateral will be Trump’s second official meeting with the Russian president in his second term, after an Alaska summit last year.
One contentious topic the Trump administration didn’t mention in its readout from the president’s last meeting with Xi is Taiwan. Chinese officials previewing APEC and Trump’s visit stressed to MS NOW in a mid-October press briefing that they continued to oppose Taiwan’s “independence” and U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.
